quote: Wie viel Rechnungs- einheiten z. B. sind nöthig, um die so und so vielte Stelle der Decimalbruch-Entwick- lung von $\pi$ zu bestimmen?
english: How many computation units, for example, are necessary to determine such-and-such a digit of the decimal expansion of π?
topic: Hilbert asks how the advantages of known arithmetic formulas (summation of arithmetic series, congruence formulas, Stirling's formula) for computing specific problems can be quantified by counting elementary operations, giving the digits of π and the computation of n! as examples.

triage.modern_statement: What is the computational complexity (counted in elementary bit or arithmetic operations, as a function of n) of computing the n-th decimal digit of π? Modern versions of the question: (a) the bit complexity of computing the first n digits of π; (b) the cost of computing only the n-th digit, without the earlier ones (digit extraction), in time and in memory. This is an early version of the idea behind computational complexity theory: comparing algorithms by how many elementary operations they need.
triage.answered_by: No one answered Hilbert's question as such. It was answered piece by piece within computational complexity and algorithms for π. Salamin and Brent (1976), using the arithmetic-geometric mean (AGM), compute n digits of π in O(M(n) log n) bit operations, where M(n) is the cost of multiplying two n-bit numbers. Bailey, Borwein and Plouffe (1995/1997), with the BBP formula, compute the n-th hexadecimal (base-16) digit without computing the earlier digits. Plouffe (1996) gave a method for the n-th decimal digit without the earlier digits. Bellard (1997) brought that to O(n^2) in any base. Whether these bounds are optimal (lower bounds) has not been settled.

evidence.claim: Salamin (1976) and the Borweins' book 'Pi and the AGM' give AGM algorithms for π that run in almost linear time, O(M(n) log n), where M(n) is the time for n-bit multiplication.
Brent's survey analyses the bit complexity of the AGM / Brent–Salamin algorithms for π.
Bailey, Borwein and Plouffe found a method that computes the N-th hexadecimal digit of π efficiently without the previous N-1 digits.
The BBP formula does not give the n-th decimal (base-10) digit.
Plouffe (Nov 1996), 'On the computation of the n-th decimal digit of various transcendental numbers', gives a method for computing the n-th decimal digit of π.
Bellard: computing the n-th digit of π in any base in O(n^2), building on Plouffe's algorithm.
Borwein, Galway and Borwein (2004) showed there are no degree-1 BBP-type formulas for π except those whose base is a power of two. So no such base-10 digit-extraction formula exists.

triage.why: The note asks how many elementary computing steps are needed to find the n-th decimal digit of π. Today that is a complexity question. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems, and there is no sign it is his 24th problem. Upper bounds have been found: almost-linear bit complexity for computing all n digits (Salamin–Brent AGM), and digit extraction without earlier digits (BBP in base 16; Plouffe and Bellard in base 10, O(n^2)). Optimal lower bounds are still unknown, and so is whether faster base-10 digit extraction is possible. The search results do not directly confirm that these open points are being actively researched. 'Solved' with medium confidence means the question has concrete answers, not that it is closed.
